name: Design a Video Streaming Service
intent: Let millions of people upload videos and watch them on any device and any connection, starting in a second or two and rarely stopping to buffer.
codeTitle: choosing a quality for each video segment
finalIntro: One video from upload to playback, including what happens when the viewer's connection gets worse.
prompt: Design a video service like YouTube or Netflix. Creators upload videos, and viewers press play on phones, laptops and TVs with connections that range from slow mobile data to fast fibre. Playback should start quickly and keep going.
functional: Upload videos of any size, including large files on weak connections
Process each upload so it plays on every kind of device
Play a video with fast start, seeking and quality that follows the connection
Show titles, thumbnails and search results for videos
Count views and keep watch history
nonFunctional: Playback starts in about two seconds and rarely stalls
Serve enormous bandwidth: many millions of people watching at once
Handle uneven demand: a few videos are watched by millions, most by almost nobody
Keep cost under control, because storage and bandwidth are the bill
Stay available when a data centre or region has a problem

firstAttempt.text: One web server with a big disk. Uploads are saved as files exactly as received, and to watch, the browser downloads the file over HTTP from the same server. It works for a handful of friends watching short clips.
limits: Original files come in every format and size, and many devices cannot play them
A viewer on a slow connection must download the big file faster than it plays, or the video stalls
One server can push only a limited amount of data, and each viewer takes a share for the whole video
Viewers far from the server see a long delay before anything plays
A large upload that fails halfway has to start again from nothing

steps.title: Upload to object storage and convert in the background
steps.problem: Uploaded files come in every format, and a failed big upload starts again from zero.
steps.fix: Uploads go in chunks, so a broken connection resumes where it stopped, into durable object storage. Saving the original puts a job on a queue, and a pool of transcoder workers converts the video into several resolutions and bitrates, cut into short segments of a few seconds each.
steps.tradeoff: Every device gets a format it can play, and the heavy work never blocks the uploader. The video is not watchable until transcoding finishes, and transcoding is the biggest compute cost in the system.

steps.title: Let the player pick the quality with a manifest (adaptive streaming)
steps.problem: A fixed-quality file stalls whenever the viewer's connection is slower than the video.
steps.fix: For each video the system publishes a small manifest that lists every quality and the address of each segment. The player downloads it, then fetches one segment at a time over ordinary HTTP, choosing the quality of the next segment from how fast the last one arrived and how much video it has buffered. This is how HLS and DASH work.
steps.tradeoff: Playback adapts to the connection and starts quickly with a low quality. Pictures get softer when the network is weak, there are many more small files to store and serve, and the quality choice logic lives in every client.

steps.title: Serve segments from a CDN close to the viewer
steps.problem: Pushing every segment from one storage location is slow for faraway viewers and cannot supply the bandwidth.
steps.fix: Segments are static files, so they cache perfectly. A content delivery network keeps copies in many locations near viewers. The player asks the nearest edge cache, which answers at once on a hit and fetches from storage on a miss, then keeps the segment for the next viewer.
steps.tradeoff: Start-up is faster and the origin only sees misses, which is where most of the bandwidth bill is saved. Caches must be filled, and the first viewer of a segment in each region pays the miss.

steps.title: Protect storage with an origin shield and warm popular videos
steps.problem: A new release makes thousands of edge caches miss the same segment at once and all hit the origin together.
steps.fix: Edge caches fetch from one middle cache layer, an origin shield, which merges simultaneous requests for the same segment into a single request to storage. Videos expected to be popular, such as a scheduled release, are pushed to the edges before anyone presses play.
steps.tradeoff: The origin sees roughly one request per segment, however many caches ask. One more hop on a miss and extra cache capacity to pay for, and predicting popularity is guesswork for user uploads.

steps.title: Keep video details in a metadata database with a cache
steps.problem: Titles, descriptions, thumbnails, permissions and search need fast structured lookups, which object storage is not built for.
steps.fix: A metadata database stores one record per video: owner, title, status, the manifest location and so on, sharded by video id. The API reads it through a cache and serves search from a separate index built from the same records. The video bytes stay in object storage and the CDN.
steps.tradeoff: Browsing is fast and the huge files stay out of the database. Metadata and files can disagree for a moment, for example a record saying a video is ready before its segments have reached every cache, so readiness is set only after processing is complete.

steps.title: Count views and watch time through an event stream
steps.problem: Updating a counter in the database every time anyone watches would overload it, and views for popular videos hit one row millions of times.
steps.fix: Players send small playback events, such as started and watched 30 seconds, into a stream. Aggregators read the stream, add up counts in batches, and write totals to the metadata store every few seconds. The same events feed watch history and recommendations.
steps.tradeoff: The database sees a trickle of batched writes, and the event data is useful for many things. View counts lag by seconds or minutes and are approximate, and the pipeline must filter duplicates and bots.

failures.impact: Segments that are not already in a cache cannot be fetched, and new uploads fail in that region.
failures.answer: Object storage replicates every video to at least two regions, so the shield and edge caches fall back to another copy. Popular segments keep playing from the edge meanwhile, and uploads are redirected to a healthy region.

failures.scenario: A transcoder crashes halfway through a video, or a file is corrupt
failures.impact: The video never becomes ready, and a bad file could crash worker after worker.
failures.answer: Jobs are retried by the queue with backoff, and each segment is written under a name derived from the video and quality, so a rerun overwrites rather than duplicates. After a few failed attempts the job moves to a dead-letter queue, the video is marked failed, and the uploader is told.

failures.scenario: A highly awaited video is released and millions press play in the same minute
failures.impact: Every edge cache misses the first segments together, which could flatten the origin.
failures.answer: The video was warmed into the edge caches before release, and the origin shield merges whatever misses remain into one request per segment. Player start-up begins at a low quality and climbs, which spreads bandwidth demand, and the CDN can fall back to a second provider.

alternatives.title: How video reaches the player

options.name: Progressive download
options.pro: Simplest: one file over plain HTTP
options.con: One quality for everyone, stalls on weak connections, wastes data if the viewer leaves

options.name: Adaptive streaming over HTTP (HLS, DASH)
options.pro: Quality follows the network, works with ordinary web servers and CDNs
options.con: Delay of several seconds behind live, and many small files

options.name: Real-time streaming (WebRTC)
options.pro: Under a second of delay, good for calls and live auctions
options.con: Hard to cache or scale to millions of viewers, so it costs much more per viewer

alternatives.pick: Adaptive HTTP streaming for videos on demand and most live events. Real-time protocols only where sub-second delay matters.

alternatives.title: Segment length

options.name: Short (about 2 seconds)
options.pro: Quick to adapt and quick to start
options.con: More requests and more overhead, and slightly worse compression

options.name: Long (about 10 seconds)
options.con: Slow to react when the connection drops, and a longer start

alternatives.pick: Four to six seconds as a balance, shorter for live.

alternatives.title: When to transcode each quality

options.name: Everything up front
options.pro: Every video is instantly ready in all qualities
options.con: Pays to encode qualities for videos that nobody will watch

options.name: On demand for the first viewer
options.pro: Saves compute for the long tail of unpopular videos
options.con: First viewer waits, and a surge can overload the encoders

options.name: Basic ladder first, more by popularity
options.pro: Quick availability, with extra effort only for videos that earn it
options.con: A policy to tune and a pipeline that must be re-runnable

alternatives.pick: A basic ladder for every video, and extra qualities and better compression as a video becomes popular.

alternatives.title: Who runs the delivery network

options.name: Commercial CDN
options.pro: Immediate global reach with no hardware to run
options.con: Per-gigabyte pricing that becomes the biggest cost at large scale

options.name: Own caches placed inside internet providers
options.pro: Lowest cost per viewer and shorter paths at very large scale
options.con: A large engineering and operations effort, justified only by huge traffic

alternatives.pick: A commercial CDN to start, and your own network only when bandwidth cost dominates.
